title: Magnetic active matter across scales
authors: Francisca Guzmán-Lastra, Margaret Rosenberg, Marco Musacchio, Lorenzo Caprini, Hartmut Löwen
abstract: Magnetic interactions provide a versatile and powerful tool for controlling and organizing active matter, where individual units continuously consume energy to drive autonomous motion. These interactions arise naturally in biological systems, such as magnetotactic bacteria, and can be engineered into synthetic platforms, including colloidal microswimmers, magnetic nanoparticles, and macroscopic granular robots. This review focuses on active, self-propelled particles that carry an intrinsic magnetic dipole moment, powered by their own energy consumption rather than driven by external fields; here, the dipole moment mediates interactions and self-organization, not propulsion. We survey experimental and theoretical studies across all length scales, showing how dipolar interactions shape single-particle dynamics, collective behavior, and self-organization. We discuss models incorporating pairwise dipolar forces and confinement, and examine emergent phenomena such as chaining, swarming, and tunable pattern formation. We close by outlining challenges and opportunities in the design, control, and application of magnetic active systems, from programmable materials and biomedical actuation to nonequilibrium physics.
summary: This review surveys magnetic active matter, detailing how intrinsic magnetic dipoles drive self-organization in systems ranging from bacteria to synthetic robots. It synthesizes theoretical models and experimental results showing that dipolar interactions are key for controlling collective behaviors like swarming and pattern formation. The work highlights the broad applicability of these principles across diverse physical scales.
main_problem: The review focuses on understanding how magnetic dipole interactions control and organize active matter across all length scales, from nanoscale particles to macroscopic robots.
main_result: Magnetic dipolar forces provide a versatile tool for achieving complex self-organization, leading to phenomena like chaining, swarming, and tunable pattern formation in non-equilibrium systems.
method: The paper surveys both theoretical models (e.g., Langevin dynamics using point dipole approximations) and experimental realizations across various physical platforms.
model_or_system: The system involves active particles carrying intrinsic magnetic dipoles whose interactions mediate self-organization, distinct from external field propulsion. Examples include magnetotactic bacteria, colloidal swimmers, and granular robots.
key_observables: Chaining, swarming, tunable pattern formation, alignment, collective hydrodynamic states (e.g., vortices), and reconfigurable structures.
important_parameters: Péclet number (Pe) comparing activity strength to diffusion; dimensionless magnetic coupling parameter ($\lambda$) comparing dipolar energy to thermal energy ($k_B T$).
main_assumptions: The point-dipole approximation is used for long-range interactions, and the dynamics are often modeled using overdamped Langevin equations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically classifies experimental realizations based on activity (Pe) and interaction strength ($\lambda$), categorizing systems into colloids, granular matter, and biological examples.
paper_structure: The review progresses by establishing the fundamental role of magnetic interactions in active matter, detailing the theoretical modeling across scales (nano to macro), surveying diverse physical implementations (bacteria, synthetic swimmers), and concluding with applications and open challenges.
why_interesting: While focused on classical non-equilibrium dynamics, the study of collective behavior, pattern formation, and energy dissipation in these systems touches upon concepts relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and complex many-body physics.
